tagline.text: The old downtown shopping street of Iloilo, lined with neoclassical and Art Deco buildings

location.label: Location
location.text: J.M. Basa Street, City Proper, Iloilo City (the old downtown commercial district)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (walk early in the morning or around sunset)

children.text: Calle Real is the nickname of J.M. Basa Street, which runs about 0.75 km through the old downtown of Iloilo City. It has been the main commercial street since Spanish times, the National Historical Commission declared it a heritage zone in 2014, and it is lined with neoclassical, Beaux-Arts and Art Deco buildings.

Calle Real is Spanish for "Royal Street," and its official name is J.M. Basa Street. It is named after José María Basa, a businessman and Propaganda Movement associate of José Rizal, but people in Iloilo still call it Calle Real. The street is about

long, with General Hughes Street at its east end and Iznart Street at its west end, and it meets Ortiz, Mapa, Guanco and Aldeguer streets. It sits in the heart of Iloilo City's old downtown, commonly called the City Proper.

The street became a commercial center in the 1800s, during the Spanish era, as Iloilo prospered as a sugar-exporting port. In the early American period it was lined with upscale shops selling European goods, and in the 20th century department stores, banks, theaters and office buildings went up in neoclassical, Beaux-Arts and Art Deco styles. Hoskyn's department store, which opened in 1877, is known as the first department store in the Philippines. Commerce later shifted to Mandurriao and Iloilo Business Park, and the street declined for a time, but since the 2010s restoration of facades, clearing of billboards and burying of utility lines have been under way.

Institutionally, it was designated one of Iloilo City's cultural heritage tourism zones in 2013, and on August 8, 2014, the National Historical Commission declared the Calle Real area a heritage zone. The district, also called the Iloilo Central Business District, covers a Heritage Core of about 14 hectares and an expanded conservation area, about 26 hectares in all. There is also a proposal to put it on the UNESCO tentative list as part of the serial nomination "The Sugar Cultural Landscape of Negros and Panay Islands." Underground cabling work that began in 2023 had removed the overhead wires along the entire street by January 2025.

This guide is for travelers who want to walk around Iloilo City and see Calle Real. No single building is a huge attraction, but if you read the construction years carved into the facades and follow the old theaters and department store sites, you can see how wealthy a port Iloilo once was. The street is still a living place with local shops and banks, so approach it as an urban walk rather than a museum. The conservation area also includes San Jose Parish Church, said to have been founded in 1607 and described as the oldest church in Iloilo City. Whether buildings are open, museum admission and event schedules can change, so it is safest to confirm the latest announcements before you visit.

Built in 1927 and once the Washington International Hotel, this building was restored in 2012. It is one of the street's signature photo spots, so look closely at the facade decoration and the construction year.

The Regent Theater was built in 1928 with a neoclassical facade, and Cine Eagle was built in 1927. The Lux Theater is said to have opened on May 7, 1922. The age of the cinemas has passed, but you can still read the atmosphere of the old movie-house street in the facade structures.

blocks.title: Javellana Building and Celso Ledesma Building

children.text: The Javellana Building, built in 1922, is neo-Renaissance in style, and the Celso Ledesma Building was built in 1923. Looking up at facades with arched windows, pilasters and cornices shows you the taste of Iloilo's wealthy families in the 1920s.

Hoskyn's, which started in 1877, is recorded as the first department store in the Philippines. You will need to check locally on the building's current condition, but the name symbolizes a street where imported goods flowed during Iloilo's sugar boom.

blocks.title: Elizalde Building and the Museum of Philippine Economic History

children.text: The bahay na bato style Elizalde Building houses the Museum of Philippine Economic History. If you want to learn about Iloilo's commerce and sugar industry, it is worth adding to your Calle Real walk. Check opening days and admission locally.

blocks.title: Iloilo Customs House and Sunburst Park

children.text: Built in 1916, the Iloilo Customs House is known as the largest customs house outside Manila and stands beside Sunburst Park. Sometimes counted as one of only three customs houses left in the Philippines, it is a building that symbolizes the trade history of a port city, and its size and dignity show even from outside.

This plaza was called Plaza Alfonso XII in the Spanish era, and the flag of the First Philippine Republic was raised here after Spain surrendered. Close to the west end of Calle Real, it makes a good starting or ending point for your walk. It is known as a National Historical Landmark.

Completed in 1928 and facing Plaza Libertad, this building was declared a National Historical Landmark on February 9, 2018. Its neoclassical facade is part of the plaza scene and a good place for photographs. It is said to have served as the Japanese Army headquarters during World War II.

items.title: 1–2 hour walking route
items.subtitle: From Plaza Libertad to Calle Real

children.text: Start in front of Iloilo City Hall and Plaza Libertad. Look around the plaza, the Masonic Temple and the customs house by Sunburst Park.
Enter Calle Real (J.M. Basa Street) and walk from Iznart Street toward General Hughes Street, reading the construction years on the building facades.
Photograph the Eusebio Villanueva Building, the theater facades and the Javellana Building.
Visit the Museum of Philippine Economic History in the Elizalde Building or rest at a cafe.
Head back toward Plaza Libertad and try Ilonggo food at a market or restaurant.
Walking the whole street takes about
30–40 minutes
, and stopping at each building makes it one to two hours. Early morning is more comfortable than the heat of midday.

items.title: Half-day downtown plan
items.subtitle: From City Hall to the Capitol

children.text: Start at the restored Iloilo City Hall and Plaza Libertad.
Walk along Calle Real and look at the old theaters, bank buildings and shops.
Head to the provincial Capitol area and visit nearby sites such as the provincial museum.
Have lunch, then continue to another district such as Jaro Cathedral or Molo Church.
Iloilo's heritage is scattered across different districts, so a taxi or Grab is convenient between areas.
There are several direct flights a day from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), and the flight takes about
1 hour 10–15 minutes
. Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
The airport is in Cabatuan, so you reach the city by taxi, Grab or an airport shuttle. Check travel time and fares locally.
Within the City Proper, a taxi or Grab is easiest. Enter Plaza Libertad or J.M. Basa Street as your destination.

Jeepneys marked "Jaro CPU", "City Proper" and "Molo Baluarte" reach or pass near Plaza Libertad, and one travel guide also mentions "Jaro Liko". Routes and fares can change, so ask the driver or check locally.

The walk from Plaza Libertad along Calle Real is described as a short route of about seven blocks. Many buildings have their construction year on the facade, so it is fun to look for them as you walk.

This is an outdoor walk, so the December–May dry season is more comfortable. Midday is hot with little shade, so walk early in the morning or around sunset. In the June–November rainy season showers are frequent, so bring an umbrella and plan around museums and cafes.
The downtown is very crowded and roads are closed during Dinagyang at the end of January, so allow plenty of travel time.

The City Proper has many mid-range hotels and guesthouses, so you can explore Calle Real on foot, while the Iloilo Business Park area has large hotels and malls. Hotel names and rates change a lot by season, so check recent reviews on a booking site.

Iloilo is known for foods such as La Paz batchoy, pancit molo and chicken inasal. Markets and restaurants are close by, so it is easy to grab a meal while walking. The Iloilo Central Market is described as an Art Deco building built in 1912. At market eateries, choose places where you can see the prices and the hygiene for yourself.
Walking early in the morning or around sunset keeps you cool and gives better photo light.
Many buildings have the construction year on the upper facade, so look up to find it.
The street is still a commercial street with cars and motorbikes, so use sidewalks and crossings and check your surroundings when taking photos.
Museums and some buildings may have irregular opening days and hours, so check by phone or social media the day before.
Combining Plaza Libertad, City Hall and the customs house in one route saves travel time.
Bring water, an umbrella and a hat, and wear comfortable shoes.
In a taxi, check whether the meter is used, and for Grab, enter your destination in the app accurately.
Photography may be restricted at bank entrances and security areas, so follow the instructions you are given.
Calle Real is a busy commercial street with real businesses. Watch for pickpockets and motorbike snatchers, and carry valuables in front of your body.
Downtown traffic is heavy and some places have no pedestrian signals, so check for vehicles carefully when crossing.
Buildings and museums with set hours may have closing days, so you could make a wasted trip. Check before you go.
Construction or facility work may restrict passage on some sections. Follow the latest local guidance.
If a taxi driver refuses the meter and demands a flat fare, take another taxi.
The information in this guide covers what could be confirmed as of 2026, and building uses and business status may change.
This central city of Western Visayas is where Calle Real forms the heart of the old downtown, within
Iloilo City
. Markets, restaurants and museums come together to make a full day.
This riverside promenade, the
Iloilo River Esplanade
, is pleasant to walk around sunset and makes a fitting end to a Calle Real walk.
This Gothic-style stone church,
Molo Church
, is a taxi ride from the old downtown and can be combined into the same day.
One of Iloilo's best-known churches,
Jaro Cathedral
is worth seeing together with Jaro Plaza. Pairing it with Calle Real on the same day gives you a broad look at the city's heritage.
